body.objective: Students will be able to explore Día de los Muertos.
body.iCan: I can explore Día de los Muertos.
successCriteria: I can describe the traditions of Día de los Muertos

body.hook: Bright orange marigolds, sugar skulls and family altars covered with photos and favourite foods: Día de los Muertos isn't a sad holiday. It's a joyful celebration of remembering loved ones.

study.title: Día de los Muertos
study.question: How and why is Día de los Muertos celebrated?
study.passage:
Background (written for this lesson from public sources):
Día de los Muertos is celebrated mainly in Mexico on 1 and 2 November, with roots in Indigenous traditions blended with Catholic All Saints' and All Souls' Days. UNESCO recognized Mexico's Indigenous festivity dedicated to the dead as part of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2008.
Families believe the spirits of loved ones return to visit, so they build an ofrenda (altar) at home with: photos of the person, their favourite foods and drinks, candles, cempasúchil (bright orange marigolds whose colour and scent are said to guide spirits), pan de muerto, calaveras de azúcar (decorated sugar skulls, often with names), and papel picado (colourful cut-paper banners). Many families visit and decorate graves at the cemetery, share food and tell stories.
La Catrina, an elegant skeleton figure, comes from early 20th-century artwork by José Guadalupe Posada and is now a popular symbol.
Respect: this is a family and cultural tradition, not Halloween.
Activity: label a diagram of an ofrenda in Spanish and explain three symbols; then share (if comfortable) how your family or culture remembers loved ones.
study.source: Summary from public sources including UNESCO.

body.objective: Students will be able to compare festivals in different countries.
body.iCan: I can compare festivals in different countries.
successCriteria: I can describe festivals from different Spanish-speaking countries
I can compare festivals using más … que, menos … que and tan … como

body.hook: Giant burning statues in Valencia, an Inca sun festival in the Andes, a tomato fight in a Spanish town: festivals across the Spanish-speaking world are as varied as the countries themselves.

study.title: Fiestas del mundo hispano
study.question: How do festivals in Spanish-speaking countries compare?
study.passage:
Festivals (written for this lesson from public sources):
Las Fallas (Valencia, España, 15–19 March): neighbourhoods build huge papier-mâché and wooden figures called ninots, some as tall as buildings. On the last night, la Cremà (19 March), they are burned in giant bonfires. UNESCO recognized Las Fallas in 2016.
Inti Raymi (Cusco, Perú, 24 June): the Festival of the Sun, an Inca celebration of the sun god Inti at the winter solstice in the southern hemisphere. Today it's re-enacted with costumes, music and dance at Sacsayhuamán, near Cusco.
La Tomatina (Buñol, España, last Wednesday of August): a giant, messy tomato fight in the streets.
Carnaval de Barranquilla (Colombia, before Lent): parades, music, dance and costumes; UNESCO-recognized.
Comparatives: Las Fallas son más grandes que La Tomatina. Inti Raymi es más antiguo que Las Fallas. La Tomatina es tan divertida como el Carnaval.
Activity: groups make a comparison chart of two festivals (country, date, origin, activities, symbols) and write five comparative sentences.
study.source: Summary from public sources including UNESCO.
discussion: Why is Inti Raymi in June?
What does each festival show about its culture?
study.product: Compare two festivals in a chart and write five comparative sentences, including one with tan … como.

body.objective: Students will be able to present a festival.
successCriteria: I can research a festival from a Spanish-speaking country
I can present it in Spanish using the present and ir a + infinitive
I can answer questions about my festival
body.hook: Your mission: become the class expert on one festival from the Spanish-speaking world and present it so vividly that everyone wants to go.

study.title: Presenta una fiesta
study.question: How do I present a festival in Spanish?
study.passage:
Project guide (written for this lesson):
Choose a festival: Día de los Muertos, Las Fallas, Inti Raymi, La Tomatina, Carnaval de Barranquilla, Semana Santa in Seville, Los Sanfermines (Pamplona), La Guelaguetza (Oaxaca), Fiestas Patrias (Chile), Noche de San Juan, Día de la Independencia in Mexico (16 September), or another with teacher approval.
Content (2 minutes): 1. ¿Qué es? ¿Dónde y cuándo se celebra? 2. ¿Cuál es el origen? 3. ¿Qué hace la gente? (La gente baila, come…, lleva…) 4. ¿Qué comidas y símbolos hay? 5. Me gustaría ir porque… / Voy a ir…
Use "se celebra" (it is celebrated): Las Fallas se celebran en Valencia en marzo.
Visuals: images and key words only.
Questions: each presenter answers two questions: ¿Cuándo es? ¿Qué comen? ¿Por qué es importante?
Rubric: content, accuracy (present and ir a), vocabulary, pronunciation, visuals, answering questions.
study.source: Original project written for this lesson.
steps: Use se celebra, the present and ir a
discussion: Why did you choose your festival?
What would you most like to do there?
What did you learn from classmates?
